title: Review: Enzyme inhibition and metabolic control; Cloning and biotechnology; Nucleotides, DNA and RNA structure; ATP
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Eduqas A-level Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: BM11#t2 term and clue written for the game; BM10a#t4 term and clue written for the game; EZ03#t3 term and clue written for the game; GR09a#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: BM10a#N.11a, BM10b#N.15, BM11#N.10a, EZ03#N.14, BM10a#N.12a, BM10b#N.6a, BM11#N.5a, BM10a#N.9, BM11#N.7, BM10a#N.8, BM11#N.2, BM10a#N.2a. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: ADP
items.clue: The product formed together with Pi when ATP reacts with water

items.label: Double helix
items.clue: Shape formed when two base-paired polynucleotide strands twist together

items.label: Tertiary structure
items.clue: Overall folding of an enzyme, altered when a molecule binds away from the substrate pocket.

items.label: Immobilised enzyme
items.clue: Catalyst held on or inside an insoluble support, so it stays behind while product flows out.

questions.stem: Which row correctly gives differences between DNA and RNA?

options.text: DNA: two strands, deoxyribose, thymine. RNA: two strands, ribose, uracil.
DNA: two strands, deoxyribose, thymine. RNA: one strand, deoxyribose, thymine.
DNA: two strands, ribose, thymine. RNA: one strand, deoxyribose, uracil.
DNA: two strands, deoxyribose, thymine. RNA: one strand, ribose and uracil.

questions.explanation: DNA is double-stranded, contains the pentose deoxyribose and has thymine; RNA is single-stranded, contains ribose and has uracil in place of thymine.

questions.stem: Two DNA molecules from two hypothetical species of bacteria each contain the same number of nucleotides, and in both, 30% of the bases are adenine, 30% thymine, 20% guanine and 20% cytosine. The two molecules carry different genetic information. Which statement best explains how this is possible?

options.text: The amino acids attached along their strands are arranged in a different order in each.
The nucleotides of each species are built around a different five-carbon sugar.
Each molecule is folded into a different three-dimensional shape that stores information.
Their nucleotides are arranged in a different order along each molecule.

questions.stem: A muscle fibre holds only enough ATP for a few seconds of hard contraction. Yet a marathon runner's leg muscles keep contracting for hours. Which statement explains this?

options.text: When its ATP runs out, the fibre switches to taking energy straight from glucose to contract.
Each ATP is used once, then broken down; a brand-new ATP is built from glucose to replace it.
ADP and Pi are rejoined into ATP again and again, using energy from respiration.
Hydrolysing ATP takes in energy, and the fibre gains its energy each time ATP is re-formed.

questions.explanation: A small pool of ATP is recycled continuously. Respiration supplies the energy for each resynthesis, so the supply never runs dry while substrate and oxygen last.

questions.stem: Methanol is not very toxic itself, but the enzyme alcohol dehydrogenase converts it into toxic products. Ethanol is also a substrate of alcohol dehydrogenase. Doctors have treated methanol poisoning by giving ethanol. Why does this reduce the harm?

options.text: Ethanol binds to an allosteric site, so the active site changes shape and methanol cannot bind.
Ethanol denatures alcohol dehydrogenase, so no methanol at all is converted.
Ethanol competes with methanol for the active site, so less methanol is converted at a time.
Ethanol binds to methanol molecules, so less methanol is free to reach the enzyme.

questions.stem: A solution of DNA is heated to 95 °C. The two strands separate, but each strand remains a continuous, intact chain of nucleotides. Which explanation is consistent with these observations?

options.text: The backbone of each strand is covalently bonded, so it survives heating that breaks the weaker hydrogen bonds between the strands.
The hydrogen bonds of the backbone are stronger than the covalent bonds between strands, so only the strands come apart.
Heating breaks the covalent bonds that join the two strands, while the hydrogen bonds within each strand stay intact.
The bases along each strand are covalently bonded to one another, which holds the strand together when the pairs separate.

questions.stem: The template strand of a gene has the base sequence TACGGA at one position. What base sequence will the mRNA transcribed from it have at that position?

options.text: AUGCCU
UACGGA
ATGCCT
CGUAAG

questions.explanation: RNA nucleotides are added by complementary base pairing with the template: A pairs with U, T with A, C with G and G with C. So TACGGA gives AUGCCU.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes a life process that ATP supplies with energy?

options.text: Water entering a root hair cell by osmosis uses ATP to cross the membrane against its gradient.
Joining amino acids into a polypeptide releases energy, which the cell holds as ATP.
Chromosomes move to the poles in mitosis without ATP, pulled by spindle fibres as they get shorter.
Pumping sodium ions out of a neuron against their concentration gradient uses ATP directly.

questions.explanation: Active transport across membranes is one of the principal uses of ATP: the sodium–potassium pump hydrolyses ATP to move ions against their concentration gradients.

questions.stem: Analysis of a sample of double-stranded DNA from a hypothetical bacterium shows that 21% of its nitrogenous bases are adenine. What percentage of its bases are cytosine?
questions.explanation: A pairs with T and C pairs with G, so T = A = 21% and A + T = 42%. That leaves 100% − 42% = 58% for C and G together, and because C = G, cytosine is 58%/2 = 29%.

questions.stem: During a sprint, the small store of ATP in muscle fibres is hydrolysed and then re-formed several times over. Which statement about the energy transfers is correct?

options.text: Hydrolysis of ATP to ADP and phosphate needs an input of energy, and re-forming ATP releases it.
Hydrolysed ATP cannot be re-formed, so each contraction needs new ATP built from a glucose molecule.
Hydrolysis of ATP releases energy; energy from respiration is needed to re-form it from ADP.
The muscle takes energy directly from glucose during the sprint; hydrolysis of ATP is a minor side reaction.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes how the two strands of a DNA double helix are held together?

options.text: By hydrogen bonds between identical bases, such as A with A, one on each strand
By covalent bonds between complementary bases, with one base on each strand
By hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, one base on each strand
By covalent bonds joining the sugar–phosphate backbones of the two strands

questions.explanation: The two strands are held together by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, one from each strand: adenine pairs with thymine and cytosine with guanine. The nucleotides within each strand are joined by covalent bonds.

questions.stem: Which statement about ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is correct?

options.text: It is a nucleotide: adenine and ribose joined to a chain of three phosphate groups.
It is a small protein that binds energy released from glucose in respiration.
It is the cell's main long-term reserve of energy, built up like glycogen.
It is destroyed once used and is rebuilt from glucose rather than from ADP.

questions.explanation: ATP is a nucleotide made of the base adenine, the pentose sugar ribose and three phosphate groups. It is the molecule that distributes energy within cells.

questions.stem: Which is a correct description of a single nucleotide?

options.text: A nitrogenous base only; the sugar and phosphate belong to the backbone.
A pentose sugar bonded to a phosphate group and to a nitrogenous base.
A phosphate group bonded to a nitrogenous base, which is bonded to a sugar.
A six-carbon sugar, glucose, bonded to a phosphate and to a base.

questions.explanation: A nucleotide has three components: a pentose sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base. The sugar is central, with the phosphate and the base each bonded to it.
